SHAP TreeExplainer analysis reveals why: perplexity and surprisal features account for 88.8\% of RF's total contribution, and three independent importance measures (Gini, permutation, SHAP) achieve strong concordance (Kendall's $W{=}0.90$, $p{<}0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:permutation}), confirming that the depth signal concentrates in distributional tail statistics rather than surface lexical patterns.
Linear probing from DeBERTa hidden states yields negative $R^2$ for both \textsc{var\_surprisal} and \textsc{p90\_ppl} (Appendix~\ref{app:feature_overlap}), indicating that PLM representation spaces lack accessible structure for these tail features.
DCOL \cite{cloc2025} reached 64.5\% (Appendix~\ref{app:dcol_iterations}); all end-to-end approaches (58--65\%) underperform feature-based methods, suggesting that depth estimation benefits from explicit distributional tail statistics that PLM representations do not readily encode.

lines: \paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.

-Our conclusions regarding feature importance and depth discriminability are limited to this $3 \times 3$ grid; generalization to instruction-tuned models, larger scales (7B+), and other decoding strategies remains to be validated.
+Our findings on feature importance and discriminability are limited to this grid; transfer to untested models, scales, or strategies is not established.
\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
